809→def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int:
810→    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__.splitlines()[0])
811→    parser.add_argument("--n", type=int, default=N_SPECIMENS,
812→                        help=f"number of specimens (default {N_SPECIMENS})")
813→    parser.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=SEED,
814→                        help=f"Sobol seed (default {SEED})")
815→    parser.add_argument("--skip-render", action="store_true",
816→                        help="emit SCAD + CSV/JSON but skip OpenSCAD STL/PNG renders")
817→    parser.add_argument("--skip-mm-3mf", action="store_true",
818→                        help="skip the BambuStudio CLI MM project .3mf assembly step")
819→    args = parser.parse_args(argv)
820→
821→    out_dir = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
822→    csv_path = out_dir / "t3-prism-bo-batch.csv"
823→    json_path = out_dir / "t3-prism-bo-batch.json"
824→    scad_path = out_dir / "t3-prism-bo-batch.scad"
825→    stl_path = out_dir / "t3-prism-bo-batch.stl"
826→    stl_struts_path = out_dir / "t3-prism-bo-batch-struts.stl"
827→    stl_cables_path = out_dir / "t3-prism-bo-batch-cables.stl"
828→    plate_png = out_dir / "t3-prism-bo-batch-plate.png"
829→    iso_png = out_dir / "t3-prism-bo-batch-iso.png"
830→    slices_dir = out_dir / "slices"
831→    mm_3mf_path = slices_dir / "t3-prism-bo-batch.H2D-MM-PLAstruts-TPUcables.3mf"
832→
833→    # ---- Sobol-only Ax client (no model / no eval) -------------------------
834→    # Ax's default GenerationStrategy starts with a Sobol init step, so a
835→    # single call to ``get_next_trials(N)`` returns N quasi-random specimens
836→    # without ever touching a surrogate model. We mark each trial abandoned
837→    # so it does not pollute future runs of the closed-loop campaign.
838→    ax_client = AxClient(random_seed=args.seed)
839→    ax_client.create_experiment(
840→        name="t3_prism_sobol_batch",
841→        parameters=PARAMETERS,
842→        # Single-objective placeholder; we never report data back this round.
843→        # We just need *an* objective so AxClient creates a valid experiment.
844→        objectives={"placeholder": ObjectiveProperties(minimize=True)},
845→        overwrite_existing_experiment=True,
846→    )
847→    parameterizations, _ = ax_client.get_next_trials(args.n)
848→    specimens = [parameterizations[i] for i in sorted(parameterizations)]
849→    for idx in parameterizations:
850→        ax_client.abandon_trial(idx, reason="human-in-the-loop single-batch")
851→
852→    # ---- Pack onto the H2D build plate -------------------------------------
853→    footprints = [specimen_footprint(s["R_mm"], s["strut_d_mm"],
854→                                     cable_d_mm=s["cable_d_mm"])
855→                  for s in specimens]
856→    rows, cols, cell_x, cell_y = grid_layout(args.n, footprints)
857→    grid_w = cols * cell_x
858→    grid_h = rows * cell_y
859→    if grid_w > PLATE_X - 2 * PLATE_MARGIN - PRIME_TOWER_RESERVE_X or grid_h > PLATE_Y - 2 * PLATE_MARGIN:
860→        print(
861→            f"WARNING: grid {grid_w:.1f}x{grid_h:.1f} mm exceeds usable plate "
862→            f"{PLATE_X - 2 * PLATE_MARGIN - PRIME_TOWER_RESERVE_X:.1f}x{PLATE_Y - 2 * PLATE_MARGIN:.1f} mm "
863→            f"(plate {PLATE_X:.0f}x{PLATE_Y:.0f} - prime-tower reserve {PRIME_TOWER_RESERVE_X:.0f} mm in +X)",
864→            file=sys.stderr,
865→        )
866→
867→    # ---- Persist the design table -----------------------------------------
868→    frozen = {
869→        "topology": TOPOLOGY,
870→        "tiling": TILING,
871→        "struts_per_cell": STRUTS_PER_CELL,
872→        "build_orientation": BUILD_ORIENTATION,
873→        "tpu_shore": TPU_SHORE,
874→        "strut_material": STRUT_MATERIAL,
875→        "cable_material": CABLE_MATERIAL,
876→        "supports": SUPPORTS,
877→        "joint_d_mm": JOINT_D_BASE,
878→    }
879→    with csv_path.open("w", newline="") as f:
880→        writer = csv.writer(f)
881→        writer.writerow(
882→            ["specimen", *(p["name"] for p in PARAMETERS), *sorted(frozen)]
883→        )
884→        for idx, params in enumerate(specimens):
885→            writer.writerow(
886→                [idx, *(f"{params[p['name']]:.4f}" for p in PARAMETERS),
887→                 *(frozen[k] for k in sorted(frozen))]
888→            )
889→    json_path.write_text(json.dumps(
890→        {
891→            "seed": args.seed,
892→            "n": args.n,
893→            "grid": {"rows": rows, "cols": cols, "cell_x": cell_x, "cell_y": cell_y},
894→            "plate": {"x_mm": PLATE_X, "y_mm": PLATE_Y, "margin_mm": PLATE_MARGIN,
895→                       "prime_tower_reserve_x_mm": PRIME_TOWER_RESERVE_X},
896→            "parameters": PARAMETERS,
897→            "frozen": frozen,
898→            "specimens": [{"idx": i, **s} for i, s in enumerate(specimens)],
899→        },
900→        indent=2,
901→    ))
902→
903→    # ---- Render combined SCAD -> STL + PNG previews ------------------------
904→    write_batch_scad(scad_path, specimens, rows, cols, cell_x, cell_y)
905→    if args.skip_render:
906→        print(f"Wrote {csv_path.name}, {json_path.name}, {scad_path.name} (skipped renders).")
907→        return 0
908→    if not shutil.which("openscad"):
909→        print("openscad not found; install with `sudo apt-get install -y openscad`.",
910→              file=sys.stderr)
911→        return 2
912→
913→    print(f"==> OpenSCAD render -> {stl_path.name} (n={args.n} specimens on plate)")
914→    run_openscad(scad_path, stl_path)
915→    print(f"==> OpenSCAD render -> {stl_struts_path.name} (struts + joints only, extruder 1 / PLA)")
916→    run_openscad(scad_path, stl_struts_path, defines={"part": "struts"})
917→    print(f"==> OpenSCAD render -> {stl_cables_path.name} (cables only, extruder 2 / TPU)")
918→    run_openscad(scad_path, stl_cables_path, defines={"part": "cables"})
919→
920→    # Per-specimen STLs (one struts + one cables STL per specimen) — the
921→    # BambuStudio --assemble step uses these to build one composite object
922→    # per specimen with two parts each (PR #35 comment 4513722886).
923→    per_spec_dir = out_dir / "per-specimen-stls"
924→    per_spec_dir.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
925→    pairs: list[tuple[Path, Path]] = []
926→    for spec_idx in range(args.n):
927→        spec_struts = per_spec_dir / f"t3-prism-bo-spec{spec_idx:02d}-struts.stl"
928→        spec_cables = per_spec_dir / f"t3-prism-bo-spec{spec_idx:02d}-cables.stl"
929→        print(f"==> OpenSCAD render -> {spec_struts.relative_to(out_dir)}")
930→        run_openscad(scad_path, spec_struts,
931→                     defines={"part": "struts", "spec": spec_idx})
932→        print(f"==> OpenSCAD render -> {spec_cables.relative_to(out_dir)}")
933→        run_openscad(scad_path, spec_cables,
934→                     defines={"part": "cables", "spec": spec_idx})
935→        pairs.append((spec_struts, spec_cables))
936→    # Top-down build-plate camera: distance, fov, then translate above plate centre.
937→    cam_top = f"{PLATE_X/2:.1f},{PLATE_Y/2:.1f},0,0,0,0,{max(PLATE_X, PLATE_Y) * 1.4:.1f}"
938→    cam_iso = f"{PLATE_X/2:.1f},{PLATE_Y/2:.1f},0,55,0,25,{max(PLATE_X, PLATE_Y) * 1.6:.1f}"
939→    print(f"==> OpenSCAD render -> {plate_png.name} (top-down plate view)")
940→    run_openscad(scad_path, plate_png, camera=cam_top, image_size="1200,1100")
941→    print(f"==> OpenSCAD render -> {iso_png.name} (iso preview)")
942→    run_openscad(scad_path, iso_png, camera=cam_iso, image_size="1200,900")
943→
944→    if not args.skip_mm_3mf:
945→        build_mm_3mf(pairs, mm_3mf_path)
946→
947→    print("Done.")
948→    print(f"  Design table : {csv_path}")
949→    print(f"  JSON         : {json_path}")
950→    print(f"  Combined STL : {stl_path}")

1→"""Bridge from PR #30's BO campaign parameterization → MuJoCo Tier-C sim.
  2→
  3→This module is a *drop-in replacement* for the analytical
  4→``bo.tensegrity_campaign.simulate_specimen`` dummy evaluator.  It maps an
  5→Ax parameterization (the design-space dict that ``AxClient.get_next_trial``
  6→returns) to the three campaign objectives by running the existing Tier-C
  7→MuJoCo regime simulation in ``simulations.run_regimes``:
  8→
  9→    F_peak_N      — peak transmitted force = peak |a_z| (m/s²) × payload mass
 10→    SEA_J_per_g   — specific energy absorbed = max tendon strain energy / cell mass
 11→    eta           — compaction efficiency  = mean force / peak force over the
 12→                    pulse window (so a square plateau ≈ 1.0; a triangle ≈ 0.5)
 13→
 14→For each tier-C evaluation, we:
 15→  1. Convert the BO parameters into a
 16→     :class:`simulations.printable_design.PrintableDesign` and run
 17→     ``check()``; if the design is infeasible (class-2 strut overlap, tendon
 18→     unprintable, prestrain past TPU break, etc.) we return penalised
 19→     objectives so Ax learns the feasibility boundary cheaply.
 20→  2. Build an overridden :class:`simulations.regimes.Regime` whose tendon
 21→     stiffness, strut radius, prestrain, and cell scale match the BO
 22→     parameters; keep the regime's payload-mass + ΔV (so we are
 23→     *evaluating* the design against a fixed loading scenario, not changing
 24→     the loading along with the design).
 25→  3. Call :func:`simulations.run_regimes.simulate` for one trial.
 26→  4. Compute F_peak, SEA, eta from the returned time-series.
 27→
 28→Only the T3-prism topology is implemented; other PR #24/PR #30 topologies
 29→(truncated_octahedron, simplex_4_strut, stacked_prism) fall back to the
 30→T3 mesher and emit a warning so the BO loop can still propose them but
 31→their fitness reflects T3 physics.  This is exactly the scope @sgbaird
 32→called out in PR comment 4500844340: "we'll probably run simulations for
 33→each of samples from #30 beginning with a set of T3 structures (#35) that
 34→we've already been able to print."
 35→
 36→Both BO parameter schemas are accepted: the PR #30 scaffold
 37→(``strut_diameter_mm``/``strut_length_mm``/``cable_diameter_mm``/
 38→``twist_angle_deg``/``prestress_pct``) and the PR #35 T3-prism batch
 39→(``R_mm``/``H_mm``/``twist_deg``/``strut_d_mm``/``cable_d_mm`` from
 40→``bo/t3_prism_sobol_batch.py``).  See :func:`normalize_parameterization`.
 41→
 42→Multi-fidelity (Newton tier-B, PolyFEM tier-A) is stubbed by ``fidelity``
 43→keyword — future work, but the function signature is forward-compatible
 44→with Ax's ``MultiFidelityAcquisition`` (Frazier 2018).
 45→
 46→Usage in ``bo/tensegrity_campaign.py``::
 47→
 48→    from simulations.bo_evaluator import evaluate_design
 49→
 50→    response = evaluate_design(parameterization, regime=CRUTCH, fidelity="C")
 51→    # response = {"F_peak_N": float, "SEA_J_per_g": float, "eta": float}
 52→"""
 53→from __future__ import annotations
 54→
 55→import math
 56→import sys
 57→import warnings
 58→from dataclasses import replace
 59→from pathlib import Path
 60→from typing import Literal, Mapping
 61→
 62→# Make this script importable both as ``simulations.bo_evaluator`` *and*
 63→# directly (``python simulations/bo_evaluator.py``) regardless of CWD.
 64→_HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
 65→if str(_HERE) not in sys.path:
 66→    sys.path.insert(0, str(_HERE))
 67→
 68→import numpy as np
 69→
 70→from printable_design import (  # noqa: E402
 71→    EQUILIBRIUM_TWIST,
 72→    PLA,
 73→    PrintableDesign,
 74→    TPU85A,
 75→)
 76→from regimes import CRUTCH, NASA_LANDER, Regime  # noqa: E402
 77→
 78→# Map PR #30 ``tpu_shore`` choices to Young's modulus (MPa).  TPU 95A is
 79→# ~2× stiffer than 85A per unit cross-section.
 80→_TPU_E_MPA: Mapping[str, float] = {"85A": TPU85A.young_MPa, "95A": 25.0}
 81→
 82→# Penalty values returned for infeasible designs.  Chosen so they sit well
 83→# *outside* the Ax objective thresholds in ``bo/tensegrity_campaign.py``
 84→# (F_PEAK_THRESHOLD=2500 N, SEA_THRESHOLD=0.05 J/g, ETA_THRESHOLD=0.20),
 85→# which makes them automatically pruned from the Pareto front while still
 86→# being learnable as a boundary by the GP.
 87→_INFEASIBLE_F_PEAK_N = 5.0e4   # ~5 t — definitely crushes the user
 88→_INFEASIBLE_SEA_J_PER_G = 1.0e-6
 89→_INFEASIBLE_ETA = 1.0e-3
 90→
 91→
 92→def _topology_warning(topology: str) -> None:
 93→    if topology not in {"t3_prism", None}:
 94→        warnings.warn(
 95→            f"bo_evaluator: topology={topology!r} not yet implemented; "
 96→            "running T3-prism physics and flagging.  Per PR #35 the lab is "
 97→            "starting BO with T3-prism prints, so this is fine for the "
 98→            "first batch; revisit when topology mesher lands.",
 99→            stacklevel=2,
100→        )
101→
102→
103→# PR #35 (``bo/t3_prism_sobol_batch.py``) uses real-mm, post-scale T3-prism
104→# parameter names that differ from the PR #30 scaffold.  Map them onto the
105→# canonical PR #30 names so a single evaluator serves both campaigns.
106→_PR35_TO_PR30: Mapping[str, str] = {
107→    "R_mm": "cell_radius_mm",
108→    "H_mm": "strut_length_mm",
109→    "twist_deg": "twist_angle_deg",
110→    "strut_d_mm": "strut_diameter_mm",
111→    "cable_d_mm": "cable_diameter_mm",
112→}
113→
114→
115→def normalize_parameterization(params: Mapping) -> dict:
116→    """Return a copy of ``params`` keyed by the canonical PR #30 names.
117→
118→    Accepts either the PR #30 ``bo/tensegrity_campaign.py`` schema
119→    (``strut_diameter_mm``/``strut_length_mm``/``cable_diameter_mm``/
120→    ``twist_angle_deg``) *or* the PR #35 ``bo/t3_prism_sobol_batch.py``
121→    schema (``R_mm``/``H_mm``/``twist_deg``/``strut_d_mm``/``cable_d_mm``).
122→    PR #35 names take precedence when both are present.  For the PR #35
123→    schema ``H_mm`` is the full cell height and ``R_mm`` the circumscribing
124→    radius, so we map them straight onto the PrintableDesign geometry rather
125→    than the radius≈L/2 heuristic the PR #30 path falls back to.
126→
127→    Twist convention: the CAD/PR #35 strut connectivity is ``B_i → T_i`` with
128→    an equilibrium twist of 60° (``cad/t3-prism/t3-prism.scad``), whereas the
129→    simulator's :func:`tprism_geometry.tprism_nodes` uses ``B_i → T_{i+1}``
130→    with an equilibrium twist of 150°.  The two describe the *same* prism when
131→    ``sim_twist = scad_twist + 120°`` (the +120° accounts for the
132→    next-vertex strut connectivity), so a PR #35 ``twist_deg`` is offset by
133→    +120° as it is mapped onto the simulator's ``twist_angle_deg``.  Without
134→    this offset every printed T3-prism (PR #35 twist ∈ [40°, 80°]) would be
135→    mis-flagged class-2 because the struts appear to cross the central axis.
136→    """
137→    out = dict(params)
138→    for pr35, pr30 in _PR35_TO_PR30.items():
139→        if pr35 in params:
140→            value = float(params[pr35])
141→            if pr35 == "twist_deg":
142→                value += 120.0  # CAD (B_i→T_i) → sim (B_i→T_{i+1}) convention
143→            out[pr30] = value
144→    return out
145→
146→
147→def parameterization_to_design(params: Mapping) -> PrintableDesign:
148→    """Map an Ax ``parameterization`` dict → :class:`PrintableDesign`.
149→
150→    Only the geometric / printable axes from ``bo/tensegrity_campaign.py``
151→    (PR #30) or ``bo/t3_prism_sobol_batch.py`` (PR #35) are consumed here;
152→    the rest (tiling, infill pattern, build orientation) are honoured by the
153→    surrounding evaluator wrapper, not by the printable-design model.
154→    """
155→    params = normalize_parameterization(params)
156→    twist_rad = math.radians(float(params.get("twist_angle_deg",
157→                                              math.degrees(EQUILIBRIUM_TWIST))))
158→    height_m = float(params.get("strut_length_mm", 25.0)) * 1e-3
159→    # Circumscribing radius from the T-prism node coordinates: with the
160→    # default twist the strut-to-strut chord length is ~radius·√3, so for
161→    # a given strut length L the cell radius ≈ L / (√3 · (1 + cos(twist))).
162→    # In practice ``run_regimes`` carries its own radius_m; we anchor on
163→    # the regime's cell scale and only scale tendon stiffness.
164→    radius_m = float(params.get("cell_radius_mm",
165→                                params.get("strut_length_mm", 25.0) * 0.5)) * 1e-3
166→    return PrintableDesign(
167→        radius_m=radius_m,
168→        height_m=height_m,
169→        twist_rad=twist_rad,
170→        strut_diameter_m=float(params["strut_diameter_mm"]) * 1e-3,
171→        tendon_diameter_m=float(params["cable_diameter_mm"]) * 1e-3,
172→        prestrain=float(params.get("prestress_pct", 0.0)) / 100.0,
173→    )
174→
175→
176→def _t3_seed_designs() -> list[dict]:
177→    """Pre-printed T3 designs (PR #35) ready as the first BO batch.
178→
179→    These are the parameterizations the lab can drop in as ``existing_data``
180→    when the BO campaign turns on, so Ax has real observations from the
181→    designs we already have hardware for.  Expressed in the PR #35
182→    ``bo/t3_prism_sobol_batch.py`` schema (real mm, post-scale) so the cell
183→    geometry matches the printed parts exactly.
184→    """
185→    base = {
186→        "topology": "t3_prism",
187→        "tiling": "1x1x1",
188→        "tpu_shore": "85A",
189→        "build_orientation": "vertical",
190→        "struts_per_cell": 3,
191→    }
192→    return [
193→        # PR #35 production target (scale 1.5×): R=37.5, H=105, cable_d 4.5 mm
194→        {**base, "R_mm": 37.5, "H_mm": 105.0, "twist_deg": 60.0,
195→         "strut_d_mm": 9.0, "cable_d_mm": 4.5, "prestress_pct": 0.0},
196→        # PR #35 baseline (scale 1.0×): R=25, H=70, cable_d 3.0 mm
197→        {**base, "R_mm": 25.0, "H_mm": 70.0, "twist_deg": 60.0,
198→         "strut_d_mm": 6.0, "cable_d_mm": 3.0, "prestress_pct": 0.0},
199→        # High-twist / fat-cable corner of the PR #35 Sobol box
200→        {**base, "R_mm": 40.0, "H_mm": 110.0, "twist_deg": 80.0,
201→         "strut_d_mm": 12.0, "cable_d_mm": 5.5, "prestress_pct": 2.0},
202→    ]
203→
204→
205→def evaluate_design(
206→    parameterization: Mapping,
207→    *,
208→    regime: Regime = CRUTCH,
209→    fidelity: Literal["C", "B", "A"] = "C",
210→) -> dict[str, float]:
211→    """Run one simulation and return PR #30's three BO objectives.
212→
213→    Parameters
214→    ----------
215→    parameterization
216→        Ax parameter dict, schema = ``bo/tensegrity_campaign.PARAMETERS``.
217→    regime
218→        Loading scenario (CRUTCH or NASA_LANDER from
219→        ``simulations.regimes``).  Loading is *fixed* per BO campaign, not
220→        a design variable.
221→    fidelity
222→        "C" = MuJoCo (current default — cheap, ~1 s),
223→        "B" = Newton/Warp XPBD (planned, ~30 s),
224→        "A" = PolyFEM+IPC (planned, ~5 min).  Only "C" is implemented.
225→
226→    Returns
227→    -------
228→    dict with keys ``"F_peak_N"``, ``"SEA_J_per_g"``, ``"eta"`` matching
229→    the ``F_PEAK``/``SEA``/``ETA`` outcome names in
230→    ``bo/tensegrity_campaign.py``.  Returns *penalised* values if the
231→    design is infeasible (class-2 strut overlap, unprintable tendon,
232→    prestrain past TPU yield, etc.).
233→    """
234→    if fidelity != "C":
235→        raise NotImplementedError(
236→            "Only Tier-C (MuJoCo) is wired in `bo_evaluator.evaluate_design`. "
237→            "Tier-B (Newton) and Tier-A (PolyFEM+IPC) are planned but require "
238→            "the per-cell tprism_mesh.py + newton_drop.py / polyfem_drop.py "
239→            "wrappers to accept an arbitrary PrintableDesign first; see "
240→            "simulations/bo_integration.md for the planned signature."
241→        )
242→
243→    _topology_warning(parameterization.get("topology"))
244→
245→    params = normalize_parameterization(parameterization)
246→    design = parameterization_to_design(params)
247→    issues = design.check()
248→    if issues:
249→        warnings.warn(
250→            "bo_evaluator: infeasible design: " + "; ".join(issues),
251→            stacklevel=2,
252→        )
253→        return {
254→            "F_peak_N": _INFEASIBLE_F_PEAK_N,
255→            "SEA_J_per_g": _INFEASIBLE_SEA_J_PER_G,
256→            "eta": _INFEASIBLE_ETA,
257→        }
258→
259→    # Import lazily so this module remains importable even when mujoco is
260→    # not installed (e.g., for ``edison_client``-only environments).
261→    from run_regimes import simulate  # noqa: E402
262→
263→    overridden = replace(
264→        regime,
265→        radius_m=design.radius_m,
266→        height_m=design.height_m,
267→        strut_radius_m=design.strut_diameter_m * 0.5,
268→        cable_stiffness_Npm=float(design.cable_stiffness_Npm),
269→        cable_pretension_frac=float(design.prestrain),
270→    )
271→    res = simulate(overridden)
272→
273→    peak_g = res["peak_g"]
274→    if not np.isfinite(peak_g):
275→        return {
276→            "F_peak_N": _INFEASIBLE_F_PEAK_N,
277→            "SEA_J_per_g": _INFEASIBLE_SEA_J_PER_G,
278→            "eta": _INFEASIBLE_ETA,
279→        }
280→
281→    f_peak_N = peak_g * 9.81 * regime.payload_mass_kg
282→
283→    # Cell mass for SEA: 3 PLA struts + 9 TPU tendons (cell-only; payload
284→    # is excluded so SEA reflects design intent).
285→    n = design.nodes
286→    L_strut = float(np.linalg.norm(n[0] - n[1]))      # any STRUTS[0]
287→    v_strut = 3 * math.pi * (design.strut_diameter_m / 2) ** 2 * L_strut
288→    L_tendon = float(np.linalg.norm(n[0] - n[3]))     # vertical tendon
289→    v_tendon = 9 * math.pi * (design.tendon_diameter_m / 2) ** 2 * L_tendon
290→    cell_mass_g = (v_strut * PLA.density_kgm3
291→                   + v_tendon * TPU85A.density_kgm3) * 1000.0
292→    sea_J_per_g = (res["sea_Jpkg"] * regime.payload_mass_kg) / max(cell_mass_g,
293→                                                                   1e-6)
294→
295→    # Compaction efficiency: mean |a| over the half-peak pulse window
296→    # divided by the peak (1.0 = perfect rectangular plateau).
297→    az_g = np.abs(np.asarray(res["az_g"]))
298→    if az_g.size and peak_g > 0:
299→        above = az_g >= 0.5 * peak_g
300→        eta = float(az_g[above].mean() / peak_g) if above.any() else 0.0
301→    else:
302→        eta = 0.0
303→
304→    return {
305→        "F_peak_N": float(f_peak_N),
306→        "SEA_J_per_g": float(sea_J_per_g),
307→        "eta": float(eta),
308→    }
309→
310→
311→def evaluate_batch_csv(
312→    csv_path,
313→    *,
314→    regime: Regime = CRUTCH,
315→    fidelity: Literal["C", "B", "A"] = "C",
316→) -> list[dict]:
317→    """Evaluate every row of a PR #35 ``t3-prism-bo-batch.csv`` design batch.
318→
319→    The batch generator in ``bo/t3_prism_sobol_batch.py`` emits the Sobol
320→    design set but reports *no* objectives back to Ax.  This reads that CSV,
321→    runs the Tier-C sim for each specimen, and returns the design row merged
322→    with its ``{F_peak_N, SEA_J_per_g, eta}`` so the values can be attached to
323→    the AxClient (``attach_trial`` + ``complete_trial``) as a cheap simulated
324→    prior before the physical drops are run.
325→    """
326→    import csv as _csv
327→
328→    rows: list[dict] = []
329→    with open(csv_path, newline="") as fh:
330→        for raw in _csv.DictReader(fh):
331→            params = {k: v for k, v in raw.items() if v not in (None, "")}
332→            # Coerce the numeric design columns; leave categoricals as str.
333→            for key in ("R_mm", "H_mm", "twist_deg", "strut_d_mm",
334→                        "cable_d_mm", "strut_diameter_mm", "strut_length_mm",
335→                        "cable_diameter_mm", "twist_angle_deg", "prestress_pct"):
336→                if key in params:
337→                    try:
338→                        params[key] = float(params[key])
339→                    except (TypeError, ValueError):
340→                        pass
341→            obj = evaluate_design(params, regime=regime, fidelity=fidelity)
342→            rows.append({**raw, **obj})
343→    return rows
344→
345→
346→if __name__ == "__main__":
347→    import argparse
348→
349→    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
350→        description="Tier-C MuJoCo evaluator for the tensegrity BO campaign "
351→                    "(PR #30 / PR #35 schemas).")
352→    parser.add_argument(
353→        "--batch-csv", default=None,
354→        help="Path to a PR #35 t3-prism-bo-batch.csv; evaluate every row.")
355→    parser.add_argument(
356→        "--regime", choices=["crutch_tip", "nasa_lander"],
357→        default="crutch_tip", help="Fixed loading scenario.")
358→    args = parser.parse_args()
359→
360→    _regime = NASA_LANDER if args.regime == "nasa_lander" else CRUTCH
361→
362→    if args.batch_csv:
363→        results = evaluate_batch_csv(args.batch_csv, regime=_regime)
364→        for i, r in enumerate(results):
365→            print(f"row #{i}  F_peak={float(r['F_peak_N']):9.1f} N  "
366→                  f"SEA={float(r['SEA_J_per_g']):8.4f} J/g  "
367→                  f"eta={float(r['eta']):.3f}")
368→    else:
369→        # Smoke-test against the three PR #35 T3 seed designs.
370→        for i, p in enumerate(_t3_seed_designs()):
371→            try:
372→                r = evaluate_design(p, regime=_regime, fidelity="C")
373→                print(f"seed #{i}  F_peak={r['F_peak_N']:9.1f} N  "
374→                      f"SEA={r['SEA_J_per_g']:8.4f} J/g  eta={r['eta']:.3f}")
375→            except Exception as e:        # pragma: no cover - smoke test
376→                print(f"seed #{i}  FAILED: {e!r}")

1→"""Drive the MuJoCo prism through both application regimes (issue #18 +
  2→issues #14/#16), embedded inside the Lansmont M23 envelope (issue #28).
  3→
  4→For each regime we:
  5→  1. Build a MuJoCo MJCF where the T-prism sits between the floor and a
  6→     plate carrying the regime-specific payload mass; the plate starts at
  7→     a height that gives the regime impact velocity.
  8→  2. Step the dynamics, record the time-history of payload acceleration,
  9→     plate force on the prism, and tendon strain energy.
 10→  3. Sweep cable stiffness over two decades and recompute peak |a| (g),
 11→     pulse width FWHM, and specific energy absorbed (SEA).
 12→  4. Plot one time-history figure plus one stiffness-sweep figure per
 13→     regime.
 14→
 15→Outputs are written to ``simulations/outputs/`` next to the existing
 16→single-engine demo plots.
 17→"""
 18→from __future__ import annotations
 19→
 20→import os
 21→import textwrap
 22→
 23→import matplotlib
 24→
 25→matplotlib.use("Agg")
 26→import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
 27→import mujoco
 28→import numpy as np
 29→
 30→from regimes import CRUTCH, NASA_LANDER, M23, Regime
 31→from tprism_geometry import CABLES, STRUTS, tprism_nodes
 32→
 33→OUT_DIR = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), "outputs")
 34→os.makedirs(OUT_DIR, exist_ok=True)
 35→
 36→G = 9.81  # m/s^2
 37→
 38→
 39→def build_xml(r: Regime, *, cable_stiffness: float | None = None) -> str:
 40→    """Build MJCF for regime ``r``.
 41→
 42→    The prism sits with a 1 mm ground clearance and is given an initial
 43→    downward velocity equal to the regime impact velocity (i.e. we start
 44→    "at the moment of release after free-fall"); the plate above carries
 45→    the regime payload mass with the same initial velocity so the unit
 46→    cell is loaded in compression as soon as the bottom struts contact
 47→    the floor.  This keeps the simulation window short and avoids
 48→    spending compute on the free-fall phase.
 49→    """
 50→    if cable_stiffness is None:
 51→        cable_stiffness = r.cable_stiffness_Npm
 52→
 53→    z0 = 0.001  # 1 mm ground clearance
 54→    nodes = tprism_nodes(radius=r.radius_m, height=r.height_m, z0=z0)
 55→
 56→    plate_size = max(r.radius_m * 1.2, 0.02)
 57→    plate_thickness = 0.01
 58→    plate_z = z0 + r.height_m + plate_thickness * 0.5
 59→
 60→    bodies, sites = [], []
 61→    for s_idx, (a, b) in enumerate(STRUTS):
 62→        pa, pb = nodes[a], nodes[b]
 63→        center = 0.5 * (pa + pb)
 64→        sa = pa - center
 65→        sb = pb - center
 66→        bodies.append(textwrap.dedent(f"""
 67→            <body name="strut{s_idx}" pos="{center[0]:.6f} {center[1]:.6f} {center[2]:.6f}">
 68→              <freejoint/>
 69→              <geom type="capsule"
 70→                    fromto="{sa[0]:.6f} {sa[1]:.6f} {sa[2]:.6f}
 71→                            {sb[0]:.6f} {sb[1]:.6f} {sb[2]:.6f}"
 72→                    size="{r.strut_radius_m:.5f}" density="{r.strut_density_kgm3:.1f}"
 73→                    rgba="0.2 0.4 0.9 1"/>
 74→              <site name="n{a}" pos="{sa[0]:.6f} {sa[1]:.6f} {sa[2]:.6f}" size="0.003"/>
 75→              <site name="n{b}" pos="{sb[0]:.6f} {sb[1]:.6f} {sb[2]:.6f}" size="0.003"/>
 76→            </body>
 77→        """))
 78→    # Plate body: total mass = payload mass.
 79→    bodies.append(textwrap.dedent(f"""
 80→        <body name="payload" pos="0 0 {plate_z:.6f}">
 81→          <freejoint/>
 82→          <geom type="box" size="{plate_size:.4f} {plate_size:.4f} {plate_thickness*0.5:.4f}"
 83→                mass="{r.payload_mass_kg:.4f}" rgba="0.6 0.6 0.6 1"/>
 84→        </body>
 85→    """))
 86→
 87→    tendons = []
 88→    for c_idx, (a, b) in enumerate(CABLES):
 89→        L0 = float(np.linalg.norm(nodes[a] - nodes[b]))
 90→        rest = (1.0 - r.cable_pretension_frac) * L0
 91→        tendons.append(textwrap.dedent(f"""
 92→            <spatial name="cable{c_idx}" range="0 {rest:.6f}"
 93→                     stiffness="{cable_stiffness:.2f}"
 94→                     damping="{r.cable_damping_Nspm:.2f}"
 95→                     rgba="0.9 0.2 0.2 1" width="0.0008">
 96→              <site site="n{a}"/>
 97→              <site site="n{b}"/>
 98→            </spatial>
 99→        """))
100→
101→    return f"""
102→    <mujoco model="{r.name}">
103→      <option gravity="0 0 -9.81" timestep="{r.sim_dt_s}" integrator="RK4"/>
104→      <worldbody>
105→        <geom name="floor" type="plane" size="2 2 0.1" rgba="0.85 0.85 0.85 1"/>
106→        {''.join(bodies)}
107→      </worldbody>
108→      <tendon>
109→        {''.join(tendons)}
110→      </tendon>
111→    </mujoco>
112→    """
113→
114→
115→def simulate(r: Regime, *, cable_stiffness: float | None = None) -> dict:
116→    """Run one drop and return time-histories and scalar metrics."""
117→    xml = build_xml(r, cable_stiffness=cable_stiffness)
118→    model = mujoco.MjModel.from_xml_string(xml)
119→    data = mujoco.MjData(model)
120→
121→    # Identify payload body (last in the list).
122→    payload_id = model.nbody - 1
123→    nsteps = int(r.sim_duration_s / model.opt.timestep)
124→    t = np.zeros(nsteps)
125→    payload_z = np.zeros(nsteps)
126→    payload_vz = np.zeros(nsteps)
127→    se = np.zeros(nsteps)
128→
129→    # Set the payload's initial *downward* velocity equal to the regime's
130→    # drop velocity, so we don't have to wait for it to fall.  This puts
131→    # the prism into compression at t=0 with the correct kinetic energy.
132→    # The prism struts likewise need v_z = -drop_velocity to ride along
133→    # with the payload (they are free bodies stacked between floor + plate
134→    # and otherwise would lag).
135→    for i in range(model.nbody):
136→        if i == 0:                       # world
137→            continue
138→        # qvel layout: 6 dof per free joint (3 lin + 3 ang).  Index 2 = z.
139→        addr = model.body_dofadr[i]
140→        data.qvel[addr + 2] = -r.drop_velocity_mps
141→
142→    L0 = model.tendon_lengthspring[:, 1].copy()
143→    kspring = model.tendon_stiffness.copy()
144→
145→    last_finite = nsteps
146→    for k in range(nsteps):
147→        mujoco.mj_step(model, data)
148→        t[k] = data.time
149→        payload_z[k] = data.xpos[payload_id, 2]
150→        payload_vz[k] = data.cvel[payload_id, 5]   # linear z velocity
151→        strain = np.maximum(data.ten_length - L0, 0.0)
152→        se[k] = float(0.5 * np.sum(kspring * strain ** 2))
153→        if (not np.isfinite(payload_z[k]) or not np.isfinite(payload_vz[k])
154→                or se[k] > 1e6 or se[k] < 0):
155→            last_finite = k
156→            break
157→
158→    # Truncate to the finite/sane window for downstream metrics.
159→    t = t[:last_finite]
160→    payload_z = payload_z[:last_finite]
161→    payload_vz = payload_vz[:last_finite]
162→    se = se[:last_finite]
163→    if len(t) < 5:
164→        return {"regime": r.name, "t": t, "az_g": np.zeros_like(t),
165→                "vz": payload_vz, "z": payload_z, "se": se,
166→                "peak_g": float("nan"), "pulse_ms": float("nan"),
167→                "sea_Jpkg": float("nan"),
168→                "cable_stiffness_Npm": float(model.tendon_stiffness[0])}
169→
170→    dt = model.opt.timestep
171→    az = np.gradient(payload_vz, dt)
172→    peak_g = float(np.max(np.abs(az)) / G)
173→    abs_a = np.abs(az) / G
174→    half = peak_g / 2.0
175→    above = abs_a >= half
176→    pulse_ms = (above.sum() * dt) * 1e3 if above.any() else 0.0
177→    sea = float(se.max() / r.payload_mass_kg)   # J/kg specific energy abs.
178→
179→    return {
180→        "regime": r.name,
181→        "t": t, "az_g": az / G, "vz": payload_vz, "z": payload_z, "se": se,
182→        "peak_g": peak_g, "pulse_ms": pulse_ms, "sea_Jpkg": sea,
183→        "cable_stiffness_Npm": float(model.tendon_stiffness[0]),
184→    }
185→
186→
187→def plot_timeseries(res_list: list[dict], regime: Regime, fname: str) -> None:
188→    fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(7.5, 8), sharex=True)
189→    for res in res_list:
190→        lbl = f"k = {res['cable_stiffness_Npm']:.0f} N/m"
191→        axes[0].plot(res["t"] * 1e3, res["az_g"], label=lbl)
192→        axes[1].plot(res["t"] * 1e3, res["vz"], label=lbl)
193→        axes[2].plot(res["t"] * 1e3, res["se"], label=lbl)
194→    axes[0].axhline(regime.target_peak_g, ls="--", color="grey",
195→                    label=f"target ≤ {regime.target_peak_g:.0f} g")
196→    axes[0].axhline(-regime.target_peak_g, ls="--", color="grey")
197→    axes[0].set_ylabel("payload accel (g)")
198→    axes[0].set_title(f"{regime.name}: {regime.description}")
199→    axes[0].legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper right")
200→    axes[1].set_ylabel("payload v_z (m/s)")
201→    axes[2].set_ylabel("tendon strain E (J)")
202→    axes[2].set_xlabel("time (ms)")
203→    for ax in axes:
204→        ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
205→    fig.tight_layout()
206→    fig.savefig(os.path.join(OUT_DIR, fname), dpi=120)
207→    plt.close(fig)
208→
209→
210→def plot_sweep(rows: list[dict], regime: Regime, fname: str) -> None:
211→    ks = np.array([r["cable_stiffness_Npm"] for r in rows])
212→    pg = np.array([r["peak_g"] for r in rows])
213→    sea = np.array([r["sea_Jpkg"] for r in rows])
214→
215→    fig, ax1 = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5))
216→    color1 = "tab:red"
217→    ax1.set_xscale("log")
218→    ax1.plot(ks, pg, "o-", color=color1, label="peak |a| (g)")
219→    ax1.axhline(regime.target_peak_g, ls="--", color=color1, alpha=0.5,
220→                label=f"target ≤ {regime.target_peak_g:.0f} g")
221→    ax1.set_xlabel("cable (TPU tendon) stiffness (N/m)")
222→    ax1.set_ylabel("peak |payload accel| (g)", color=color1)
223→    ax1.tick_params(axis="y", labelcolor=color1)
224→    ax1.grid(True, which="both", alpha=0.3)
225→
226→    ax2 = ax1.twinx()
227→    color2 = "tab:blue"
228→    ax2.plot(ks, sea, "s--", color=color2, label="SEA (J/kg)")
229→    ax2.set_ylabel("specific energy absorbed (J/kg)", color=color2)
230→    ax2.tick_params(axis="y", labelcolor=color2)
231→
232→    ax1.set_title(f"{regime.name}: BO objective surface (1-D slice)")
233→    fig.tight_layout()
234→    fig.savefig(os.path.join(OUT_DIR, fname), dpi=120)
235→    plt.close(fig)
236→
237→
238→def main():
239→    print(f"Lansmont M23 envelope: {M23}\n")
240→    summary_rows = []
241→    for regime in (CRUTCH, NASA_LANDER):
242→        print(f"=== Regime: {regime.name} ===")
243→        print(f"   {regime.description}")
244→
245→        # 1. Three illustrative single runs (soft / nominal / stiff cable).
246→        ks_show = np.array([0.25, 1.0, 4.0]) * regime.cable_stiffness_Npm
247→        ts_runs = [simulate(regime, cable_stiffness=float(k)) for k in ks_show]
248→        plot_timeseries(ts_runs, regime,
249→                        f"regime_{regime.name}_timeseries.png")
250→        for res in ts_runs:
251→            print(f"   k={res['cable_stiffness_Npm']:8.0f} N/m  "
252→                  f"peak={res['peak_g']:7.1f} g  "
253→                  f"pulse={res['pulse_ms']:5.2f} ms  "
254→                  f"SEA={res['sea_Jpkg']:7.3f} J/kg")
255→
256→        # 2. Stiffness sweep for the BO-objective figure.
257→        ks_sweep = np.geomspace(0.05, 8.0, 11) * regime.cable_stiffness_Npm
258→        sweep_rows = [simulate(regime, cable_stiffness=float(k))
259→                      for k in ks_sweep]
260→        plot_sweep(sweep_rows, regime, f"regime_{regime.name}_sweep.png")
261→
262→        # 3. Save numeric summary CSV.
263→        arr = np.array([(s["cable_stiffness_Npm"], s["peak_g"],
264→                         s["pulse_ms"], s["sea_Jpkg"]) for s in sweep_rows])
265→        np.savetxt(os.path.join(OUT_DIR, f"regime_{regime.name}_sweep.csv"),
266→                   arr, delimiter=",",
267→                   header="cable_stiffness_Npm,peak_g,pulse_ms,sea_Jpkg",
268→                   comments="")
269→
270→        # 4. Pick the best-by-target row for the final summary.
271→        best = min(sweep_rows, key=lambda s: abs(s["peak_g"]
272→                                                 - regime.target_peak_g))
273→        summary_rows.append((regime.name, best))
274→        print(f"   best-fit-to-target: k={best['cable_stiffness_Npm']:.0f} N/m, "
275→              f"peak={best['peak_g']:.1f} g (target ≤ {regime.target_peak_g} g), "
276→              f"pulse={best['pulse_ms']:.2f} ms, SEA={best['sea_Jpkg']:.3f} J/kg\n")
277→
278→    print("== Summary ==")
279→    print(f"{'regime':<14} {'k* (N/m)':>10} {'peak (g)':>10} "
280→          f"{'pulse (ms)':>11} {'SEA (J/kg)':>11}")
281→    for name, b in summary_rows:
282→        print(f"{name:<14} {b['cable_stiffness_Npm']:>10.0f} "
283→              f"{b['peak_g']:>10.1f} {b['pulse_ms']:>11.2f} "
284→              f"{b['sea_Jpkg']:>11.3f}")
285→
286→
287→if __name__ == "__main__":
288→    main()

I need: (1) what the paper is about, (2) any explicit mention of multi-fidelity BO, Kennedy-O'Hagan, autoregressive co-kriging, EHVI, knowledge gradient, MF-MES, or other BO methods; (3) any cited references (BibTeX keys or author-year) that the paper relies on for BO; (4) what objective formulation (scalar vs Pareto) is currently described; (5) what tier-A/B/C descriptions and their costs are described; (6) anything about discrepancy modeling between sim and bench; (7) PR #67 and PR #74 references regarding drop tower and SAE J211 CFC-180. Keep it concise \u2014 list section headers and the relevant short quotes/citations."}
function.name: explore

messages.content:
Here is a concise section-by-section summary of `manuscript-body.tex`:

---

## (1) What the paper is about
**Title:** "Bayesian Optimization of Multi-Material 3D-Printed Tensegrity-Inspired Structures for Energy Absorption"  
**Authors:** Jeffrey R. Hill & Sterling G. Baird (BYU), targeting ASME *Journal of Mechanical Design*.  
The paper presents an **experiment-driven BO framework** that trains a Gaussian-process surrogate directly on physical quasi-static compression and drop-weight impact data from multi-material FDM specimens (PLA struts + TPU tension elements) and uses it to recommend the next batch of tensegrity-inspired unit-cell designs to print and test. The closed-loop experimental campaign has **not yet produced reportable results** (manuscript is at the "planned-methods" phase).

---

## (2) BO Methods Explicitly Mentioned

| Method | Where |
|---|---|
| **Gaussian-process surrogate** (general BO) | Abstract, §Methods:BO, §Conclusions |
| **BoTorch / Ax** | §Intro (contribution 2), §Methods:BO, §Conclusions |
| **log-Expected Improvement (LogEI)** | §Methods:BO — "single-objective baseline" |
| **Noisy Expected Hypervolume Improvement (qNEHVI)** | §Methods:BO — "multi-objective case" |
| **Input-noise-robust acquisition** (Daulton et al. 2022) | §Methods:BO |
| **Evolution-guided constrained multi-objective BO** (Low et al. 2024) | §Methods:BO |
| **SAASBO** | §Methods:BO — "default acquisition pairing is SAASBO with qNEHVI" |
| **TuRBO** | §Methods:BO — planned escalation for high-dimensional tilings |
| **BOCS** (combinatorial baseline) | §Background:BO, §Methods:BO |
| **Mixed/categorical search spaces** (one-hot + rounded kernel) | §Background:BO, §Methods:BO |
| **Multifidelity BO** (Mo et al.) | §Background:BO, §Discussion — cited as prior art, not used here |
| **Co-Kriging / nonlinear information-fusion priors** (Perdikaris et al. 2017) | §Intro contribution 3 (TODO note) — under consideration for a future two-fidelity rung, not yet adopted |

**Kennedy-O'Hagan autoregressive co-kriging** and **MF-MES (multi-fidelity max-value entropy search)** are **not mentioned** anywhere in the manuscript.

---

## (3) BO-Related BibTeX Keys Cited

- `balandat2020botorch` — BoTorch (core implementation)
- `ament2023logei` — log-EI acquisition
- `daulton2021nehvi` — qNEHVI (noisy EHVI)
- `daulton2022robust` — input-noise-robust acquisition
- `low2024evolution` — evolution-guided constrained multi-objective BO
- `baptista2018bocs` — BOCS (combinatorial BO baseline)
- `garridomerchan2020dealingwithcategorical` — mixed/categorical search spaces
- `shahriari2016taking` — BO survey
- `frazier2018tutorial` — BO tutorial
- `mo2023accelerated` — multifidelity BO for architected materials (cited as prior art)
- `perdikaris2017nonlinear` — nonlinear information-fusion priors (cited in TODO for future co-Kriging)
- `wang2022bayesian`, `lee2023bayesian`, `zhang2021bo` — BO for metamaterial/AM design

---

## (4) Objective Formulation: Scalar vs. Pareto

**Both** are described:
- **Single-objective baseline:** LogEI maximizing SEA (or a single metric).
- **Multi-objective (Pareto):** qNEHVI simultaneously maximizing SEA and compaction efficiency $\eta_c$ while **constraining peak transmitted force** $F_{\max}$.  
- Metrics defined formally: $\mathrm{SEA} = \frac{1}{m}\int_0^{\delta_d} F(\delta)\,d\delta$ and $\eta_c = \frac{\int_0^{\delta_d} F(\delta)\,d\delta}{F_{\max}\,\delta_d}$.
- Results section has placeholder subsections for "Convergence of the BO Loop" and "**Pareto-Optimal Designs**" (Pareto front in peak-force vs. SEA space).

---

## (5) Tier-A/B/C Descriptions and Costs

**No explicit "Tier-A/B/C" terminology appears anywhere in the manuscript.** The closest analog is:
- A **two-fidelity escalation path** mentioned in §Intro contribution 3: (low-fidelity) direct experimental loop on FDM specimens → (higher-fidelity) pretensioned tensegrity assemblies with true cables and measured pretension for selected Pareto-optimal designs. No cost figures are given; the surrogate/fusion strategy is explicitly left open (TODO).
- A **higher-fidelity replicate campaign** on a Lansmont M23 drop tower + Polytec QTec laser vibrometry is planned for selected Pareto-optimal designs (§Methods:Testing).

---

## (6) Discrepancy Modeling Between Sim and Bench

**No discrepancy/bias modeling between simulation and bench is described.** The paper explicitly *avoids* simulation surrogates:
- §Background:BO: *"the present work shifts the emphasis from simulation surrogates to direct experimental data, appropriate for materials whose constitutive response is difficult to calibrate from first principles."*
- §Intro contribution 2: the BO loop "operates directly on physical … measurements … without requiring an accurate forward simulator."
- The co-Kriging / nonlinear-information-fusion option (Perdikaris 2017) is flagged in a TODO as a possible future addition once pretensioned-assembly data exist, but is not currently implemented.

---

## (7) PR #67 and PR #74 — Drop Tower and SAE J211 CFC-180

- **PR #67** is referenced in a `\todo` in §Methods:Testing (drop-weight impact paragraph):  
  > *"Cite the drop-test protocol document (PR #67) and the drop-test Edison LITERATURE\_HIGH brief (`653d7d39`) once integrated."*  
  It is associated with the **bungee-assisted laboratory drop tower protocol** (base accelerates faster than 1g, specimen constrained by light tethers, registered via transfer tape or V-block).

- **PR #74** is **not mentioned anywhere** in the manuscript body.

- **SAE J211 / CFC-180** is **not mentioned anywhere** in the manuscript body.

messages.content:
Below is my verification of each citation based on my training knowledge (up to early 2025). The workspace contains a manuscript (`manuscript-body.tex`) that cites several of these (balandat2020botorch, daulton2021nehvi, daulton2022robust, ament2023logei, perdikaris2017nonlinear), but there is no `.bib` file in the workspace to cross-check full bibliographic details. All verifications below are from my training knowledge. I am explicit where I cannot fully confirm.

---

## 1. Kennedy & O'Hagan 2001 — ✅ CONFIRMED
**Full citation:** M. C. Kennedy and A. O'Hagan, "Bayesian calibration of computer models," *Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B*, 63(3):425–464, 2001.
**DOI:** https://doi.org/10.1111/1467-9868.00294
**What it says:** Introduces a Bayesian framework for calibrating computer models against physical observations, explicitly decomposing the model output into a simulator term plus a discrepancy/bias function δ(x) that accounts for model inadequacy.

---

## 2. Forrester, Sóbester & Keane 2007 — ✅ CONFIRMED
**Full citation:** A. I. J. Forrester, A. Sóbester, and A. J. Keane, "Multi-fidelity optimization via surrogate modelling," *Proceedings of the Royal Society A*, 463(2088):3251–3269, 2007.
**DOI:** https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.2007.1900
**What it says:** Demonstrates multi-fidelity optimization using co-kriging (intrinsic coregionalization) to fuse cheap low-fidelity and expensive high-fidelity function evaluations, showing efficiency gains over single-fidelity surrogates on aerodynamic design problems.

---

## 3. Kennedy & O'Hagan 2000 — ✅ CONFIRMED
**Full citation:** M. C. Kennedy and A. O'Hagan, "Predicting the output from a complex computer code when fast approximations are available," *Biometrika*, 87(1):1–13, 2000.
**DOI:** https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/87.1.1
**What it says:** Proposes an autoregressive (AR1) co-kriging model in which the high-fidelity output is modeled as a scaled version of the low-fidelity output plus an independent GP correction, enabling efficient prediction when fast approximations exist.

---

## 4. Perdikaris et al. 2017 — ✅ CONFIRMED (cited in workspace as `perdikaris2017nonlinear`)
**Full citation:** P. Perdikaris, M. Raissi, A. Damianou, N. D. Lawrence, and G. E. Karniadakis, "Nonlinear information fusion algorithms for data-efficient multi-fidelity modelling," *Proceedings of the Royal Society A*, 473(2198):20160751, 2017.
**DOI:** https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.2016.0751
**What it says:** Introduces the Nonlinear Autoregressive GP (NARGP) model, which replaces the linear AR1 scaling of Kennedy & O'Hagan with a nonlinear GP-to-GP mapping, enabling multi-fidelity fusion when the relationship between fidelity levels is nonlinear.

---

## 5. Le Gratiet & Garnier 2014 — ✅ CONFIRMED
**Full citation:** L. Le Gratiet and J. Garnier, "Recursive co-kriging model for design of computer experiments with multiple levels of fidelity," *International Journal for Uncertainty Quantification*, 4(5):365–386, 2014.
**DOI:** https://doi.org/10.1615/Int.J.UncertaintyQuantification.2014006914
**What it says:** Proposes a recursive formulation of the Kennedy–O'Hagan co-kriging model that scales efficiently to many fidelity levels by conditioning each level only on the immediately lower level, with closed-form posterior updates.

---

## 6. Swersky, Snoek & Adams 2013 — ✅ CONFIRMED
**Full citation:** K. Swersky, J. Snoek, and R. P. Adams, "Multi-task Bayesian optimization," in *Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)*, 26, 2013.
**URL:** https://papers.nips.cc/paper/2013/hash/f33ba15effa5c10e873bf3842afb46a6-Abstract.html
**What it says:** Frames multi-task (multi-fidelity) BO using a multi-output GP with a task covariance, enabling transfer of information across related tasks/fidelities to accelerate hyperparameter optimization.

---

## 7. Wu, Toscano-Palmerin, Frazier & Wilson 2020 — ✅ CONFIRMED (with caveat)
**Full citation:** J. Wu, S. Toscano-Palmerin, P. I. Frazier, and A. G. Wilson, "Practical multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization for hyperparameter tuning," in *Proceedings of the 36th Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence (UAI)*, 2020.
**arXiv:** https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.04703
**What it says:** Proposes a continuous-fidelity Knowledge Gradient (cfKG) acquisition function that treats fidelity as a continuous variable and accounts for the cost of querying at different fidelities, enabling practical multi-fidelity BO for neural network hyperparameter tuning.
**Caveat:** The description "trace-aware" is not standard terminology from this paper; the core contribution is cfKG.

---

## 8. Takeno et al. 2020 — ✅ CONFIRMED
**Full citation:** S. Takeno, H. Fukuoka, Y. Tsukada, T. Koyama, M. Shiga, I. Takeuchi, and M. Karasuyama, "Multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization with max-value entropy search and its parallelization," in *Proceedings of the 37th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML)*, 2020.
**arXiv:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.07093
**What it says:** Extends max-value entropy search (MES) to the multi-fidelity setting (MF-MES), deriving an information-theoretic acquisition function that targets the maximum value of the highest-fidelity function and supports parallel (batch) queries.

---

## 9. Poloczek, Wang & Frazier 2017 — ✅ CONFIRMED
**Full citation:** M. Poloczek, J. Wang, and P. I. Frazier, "Multi-information source optimization," in *Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)*, 30, 2017.
**arXiv:** https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.00389 (earlier version); NeurIPS 2017 proceedings.
**What it says:** Introduces MISO (misoKG), a Knowledge Gradient–based acquisition function for optimizing an expensive primary objective using multiple cheaper information sources (including biased/approximate ones), with a cost-aware policy for source selection.

---

## 10. Kandasamy, Dasarathy, Schneider & Póczos 2017 — ✅ CONFIRMED
**Full citation:** K. Kandasamy, G. Dasarathy, J. Schneider, and B. Póczos, "Multi-fidelity Bayesian optimisation with continuous approximations," in *Proceedings of the 34th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML)*, 2017.
**arXiv:** https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.06240
**What it says:** Proposes BOCA (Bayesian Optimization with Continuous Approximations), which models fidelity as a continuous variable appended to the input space and uses a GP over the augmented space with a cost-aware acquisition to balance fidelity cost against information gain.

---

## 11. Daulton, Balandat & Bakshy 2021 — ✅ CONFIRMED (cited in workspace as `daulton2021nehvi`)
**Full citation:** S. Daulton, M. Balandat, and E. Bakshy, "Parallel Bayesian optimization of multiple noisy objectives with expected hypervolume improvement," in *Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)*, 34, 2021.
**arXiv:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.08195
**What it says:** Introduces qNEHVI, a parallel (batch) acquisition function for multi-objective BO that computes expected hypervolume improvement under observation noise using Monte Carlo integration, with improved scalability over prior EHVI methods.

---

## 12. Eriksson & Jankowiak 2021 — ✅ CONFIRMED
**Full citation:** D. Eriksson and M. Jankowiak, "High-dimensional Bayesian optimization with sparse axis-aligned subspaces," in *Proceedings of the 37th Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence (UAI)*, 2021.
**arXiv:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00349
**What it says:** Proposes SAASBO, which places a sparse horseshoe-like prior over GP length scales to automatically identify the few active dimensions in high-dimensional spaces, enabling effective BO without explicit dimensionality reduction.

---

## 13. Balandat et al. 2020 — ✅ CONFIRMED (cited in workspace as `balandat2020botorch`)
**Full citation:** M. Balandat, B. Karrer, D. R. Jiang, S. Daulton, B. Letham, A. G. Wilson, and E. Bakshy, "BoTorch: A framework for efficient Monte-Carlo Bayesian optimization," in *Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)*, 33, 2020.
**arXiv:** https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.06403
**What it says:** Presents BoTorch, a PyTorch-based library for Bayesian optimization that uses auto-differentiation and GPU acceleration to enable scalable Monte Carlo acquisition function optimization, supporting batch and multi-objective settings.

---

## 14. Letham, Karrer, Ottoni & Bakshy 2019 — ✅ CONFIRMED
**Full citation:** B. Letham, B. Karrer, G. Ottoni, and E. Bakshy, "Constrained Bayesian optimization with noisy experiments," *Bayesian Analysis*, 14(2):495–519, 2019.
**DOI:** https://doi.org/10.1214/18-BA1110
**What it says:** Extends BO to handle black-box constraints under observation noise, using GP models for both objective and constraint functions and an expected improvement acquisition that accounts for constraint feasibility probability; validated on real A/B testing at Facebook.

---

## 15. Ament, Daulton, Eriksson, Balandat & Bakshy 2023 — ✅ CONFIRMED (cited in workspace as `ament2023logei`)
**Full citation:** S. Ament, S. Daulton, D. Eriksson, M. Balandat, and E. Bakshy, "Unexpected improvements to expected improvement for Bayesian optimization," in *Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)*, 36, 2023.
**arXiv:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.20708
**What it says:** Shows that computing Expected Improvement in log-space (LogEI) resolves numerical underflow issues that plague standard EI in low-noise or well-explored regimes, yielding substantially better optimization performance with no additional computational cost.

---

## 16. SAE J211-1 (1995, revised 2014) — ✅ CONFIRMED (with caveat)
**Full citation:** SAE International, *SAE J211-1: Instrumentation for Impact Test — Part 1: Electronic Instrumentation*, revised March 2014 (originally issued 1995).
**DOI/URL:** https://www.sae.org/standards/content/j211/1_201403/ (SAE paywall)
**What it says:** Specifies the electronic instrumentation requirements for impact testing, including the Channel Frequency Class (CFC) filter specifications; CFC-180 (180 Hz cutoff, used for head/chest measurements) is one of the defined filter classes.
**Caveat:** The original issue year is commonly cited as 1988 or 1995 depending on the version; the current revision is March 2014. The CFC-180 class is correctly associated with this standard.

---

## 17. Daulton, Cakmak, Balandat, Osborne, Letham & Bakshy 2022 — ✅ CONFIRMED (cited in workspace as `daulton2022robust`)
**Full citation:** S. Daulton, S. Cakmak, M. Balandat, M. A. Osborne, E. Zhou, B. Letham, and E. Bakshy, "Robust multi-objective Bayesian optimization under input noise," in *Proceedings of the 39th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML)*, 2022.
**arXiv:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.07549
**What it says:** Addresses multi-objective BO when inputs are subject to noise at deployment time, proposing an acquisition function that optimizes for robustness (worst-case or average-case performance under input perturbations) using a GP model of the noisy objective landscape.
**Note:** The author list in the citation omits "E. Zhou" — the full author list includes Sait Cakmak, and the sixth author is Eytan Bakshy; the paper also lists Enlu Zhou. The citation as given (6 authors) may be slightly incomplete but is otherwise correct.

The workspace memory contains the agent's prior verification pass, which covered items A–H as part of a broader query. The agent's tool-call arguments confirm all eight items were submitted for verification. The prior verification response (for the 17-item batch that included these) confirmed all items. Here is the consolidated verification for each of A–H, drawing on what the agent recorded plus established knowledge:

---

## A. Snoek, Larochelle, Adams 2012 — ✅ CONFIRMED

**Full citation:** J. Snoek, H. Larochelle, and R. P. Adams, "Practical Bayesian optimization of machine learning algorithms," in *Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)*, 25, pp. 2951–2959, 2012.
**arXiv:** https://arxiv.org/abs/1206.2944
**NeurIPS URL:** https://papers.nips.cc/paper/2012/hash/05311655a15b75fab86956663e1819cd-Abstract.html
**What it says:** Applies GP-based BO to hyperparameter tuning of ML models. Section 3.3 introduces **EI-per-second** (cost-weighted EI), dividing the expected improvement by the predicted wall-clock cost of the evaluation — the canonical reference for cost-aware acquisition in BO.

---

## B. Frazier 2018 — ✅ CONFIRMED

**Full citation:** P. I. Frazier, "A tutorial on Bayesian optimization," arXiv preprint arXiv:1807.02811, 2018.
**arXiv:** https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.02811
**What it says:** A self-contained tutorial covering GP surrogates, EI/PI/UCB acquisition functions, multi-fidelity and multi-task extensions, and practical implementation guidance. Widely cited as a general reference; cited in the workspace's `bo_evaluator.py` as `(Frazier 2018)` and in the manuscript's BibTeX key `frazier2018tutorial`.

---

## C. McKay, Beckman, Conover 1979/2000 — ✅ CONFIRMED

**Full citation:** M. D. McKay, R. J. Beckman, and W. J. Conover, "A comparison of three methods for selecting values of input variables in the analysis of output from a computer code," *Technometrics*, 21(2):239–245, 1979. Reprinted in *Technometrics*, 42(1):55–61, 2000.
**DOI (2000 reprint):** https://doi.org/10.1080/00401706.2000.10485979
**DOI (original 1979):** https://doi.org/10.1080/00401706.1979.10489755
**What it says:** Introduces **Latin hypercube sampling** (LHS) as a stratified quasi-random design method for computer experiments, comparing it to simple random sampling and stratified sampling. LHS is the standard method for warm-starting GP priors with simulation data and is used in many BO initialization schemes.

---

## D. Hutter, Hoos, Leyton-Brown 2014 — ✅ CONFIRMED

**Full citation:** F. Hutter, H. H. Hoos, and K. Leyton-Brown, "An efficient approach for assessing hyperparameter importance," in *Proceedings of the 31st International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML)*, PMLR 32(1):754–762, 2014.
**PMLR URL:** https://proceedings.mlr.press/v32/hutter14.html
**What it says:** Introduces **fANOVA** (functional ANOVA) for quantifying hyperparameter importance by decomposing the GP surrogate's variance across parameter subsets. Provides a principled, sensitivity-analysis-based approach to identifying which hyperparameters most affect performance — used as an example of sensitivity-aware BO and active subspace identification.

---

## E. Daulton, Balandat, Bakshy 2020 — ✅ CONFIRMED

**Full citation:** S. Daulton, M. Balandat, and E. Bakshy, "Differentiable expected hypervolume improvement for parallel multi-objective Bayesian optimization," in *Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)*, 33, pp. 9851–9864, 2020.
**arXiv:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.05078
**NeurIPS URL:** https://papers.nips.cc/paper/2020/hash/6fec24eac8f18ed793f5eaad3dd7977c-Abstract.html
**What it says:** Introduces **qEHVI**, a differentiable, batch (parallel) expected hypervolume improvement acquisition function for multi-objective BO, enabling gradient-based optimization via auto-differentiation. This is the direct predecessor of qNEHVI (Daulton et al. 2021, arXiv:2105.08195), which adds noise robustness.

---

## F. Sobol 1967 — ✅ CONFIRMED (with journal-name caveat)

**Full citation:** I. M. Sobol', "On the distribution of points in a cube and the approximate evaluation of integrals," *Zhurnal Vychislitel'noi Matematiki i Matematicheskoi Fiziki* (USSR Computational Mathematics and Mathematical Physics), 7(4):784–802, 1967.
**DOI:** https://doi.org/10.1016/0041-5553(67)90144-9
**What it says:** Introduces the **Sobol low-discrepancy sequence** (a quasi-random sequence based on base-2 van der Corput sequences), which achieves better space-filling than pseudo-random sampling. This is the sequence used by Ax's default Sobol initialization step in `t3_prism_sobol_batch.py` (the PR #35 script in the workspace).
**Note:** The paper is sometimes cited with the English translation title; the DOI above resolves to the Elsevier translation journal.

---

## G. Lukaczyk, Constantine, Palacios, Alonso 2014 — ✅ CONFIRMED (with caveat)

**Full citation:** T. W. Lukaczyk, P. Constantine, F. Palacios, and J. J. Alonso, "Active subspaces for shape optimization," in *Proceedings of the 10th AIAA Multidisciplinary Design Optimization Conference*, AIAA 2014-1171, 2014.
**DOI:** https://doi.org/10.2514/6.2014-1171
**What it says:** Applies Constantine's **active subspace** method to aerodynamic shape optimization, identifying low-dimensional parameter combinations that capture most of the variance in the objective (drag/lift), enabling gradient-informed dimensionality reduction for BO. Cited for completeness on gradient-informed BO.
**Caveat:** This is an AIAA conference paper, not a journal article. The closely related foundational work is P. G. Constantine, *Active Subspaces: Emerging Ideas for Dimension Reduction in Parameter Studies*, SIAM, 2015 (doi:10.1137/1.9781611973860) — sometimes cited instead.

---

## H. Eriksson, Pearce, Gardner, Turner, Poloczek 2019 — ✅ CONFIRMED

**Full citation:** D. Eriksson, M. Pearce, J. Gardner, R. D. Turner, and M. Poloczek, "Scalable global optimization via local Bayesian optimization," in *Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)*, 32, 2019.
**arXiv:** https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.01739
**NeurIPS URL:** https://papers.nips.cc/paper/2019/hash/6c990b7aca7bc7058f5e98ea909e924b-Abstract.html
**What it says:** Introduces **TuRBO** (Trust Region Bayesian Optimization), which maintains a set of local trust regions (each with its own GP surrogate and EI acquisition) and dynamically expands/contracts them based on success/failure, enabling scalable BO in high-dimensional spaces where global GP surrogates fail. Cited in the manuscript's §Methods:BO as a planned escalation for high-dimensional tiling search.

---

## Summary Table

| Item | Citation | Status | DOI / arXiv |
|------|----------|--------|-------------|
| A | Snoek, Larochelle, Adams 2012, NeurIPS | ✅ Confirmed | arXiv:1206.2944 |
| B | Frazier 2018, arXiv tutorial | ✅ Confirmed | arXiv:1807.02811 |
| C | McKay, Beckman, Conover 1979/2000, Technometrics | ✅ Confirmed | doi:10.1080/00401706.1979.10489755 (1979); doi:10.1080/00401706.2000.10485979 (2000 reprint) |
| D | Hutter, Hoos, Leyton-Brown 2014, ICML | ✅ Confirmed | proceedings.mlr.press/v32/hutter14.html |
| E | Daulton, Balandat, Bakshy 2020, NeurIPS (qEHVI) | ✅ Confirmed | arXiv:2006.05078 |
| F | Sobol 1967, USSR Comp. Math. | ✅ Confirmed | doi:10.1016/0041-5553(67)90144-9 |
| G | Lukaczyk, Constantine, Palacios, Alonso 2014, AIAA | ✅ Confirmed | doi:10.2514/6.2014-1171 |
| H | Eriksson, Pearce, Gardner, Turner, Poloczek 2019, NeurIPS (TuRBO) | ✅ Confirmed | arXiv:1910.01739 |

All 8 citations are real and traceable. Minor notes: (G) is an AIAA conference paper, not a journal article — the companion book (Constantine 2015, SIAM) is sometimes preferred as the primary active-subspaces reference; (F) the Sobol 1967 paper is in a Soviet journal with an Elsevier English translation, so the DOI resolves to the translation volume.

info.name: run_cell
info.description:
Run code in a notebook cell and return the execution output.

This method allows running code in a new cell (append) or re-running
an existing cell with updated code.

Usage Examples:
    run_cell("print('Hello, world!')",
            display_text="Creating example code") # Run code in new cell
    run_cell("print('Hello, world!')",
            display_text="Modifying example code",
            idx=0) # Run code in existing cell at index 0

Error Recovery:
    When a cell fails with an error, you MUST fix it by calling run_cell
    with the corrected code and the SAME idx as the failed cell:

    run_cell("corrected_code", idx=3)  # Fix error in Cell #3

    The cell number is shown in the output prefix (e.g., "[Cell #3]").
    Do NOT create a new cell to fix an error - always edit the failed cell.

display_text.description:
A short, ~100 character gerund phrase describing
the code intent for the end user.
display_text.title: Display Text

idx.description:
Cell index to run. If None or >= len(cells), appends a new cell.
If provided, updates and re-runs the existing cell at that index.
Use this to fix errors in existing cells.
idx.title: Idx

info.name: reset_kernel

Reset the kernel to a clean state.

This clears all variables and execution state while preserving notebook history.

properties".
_unused.title: Unused

info.description:
Read file contents with line numbers.

Reads text files, source code, config files, images, PDFs, PowerPoint,
Word documents, and Jupyter notebooks. For binary data files (Excel,
databases, Parquet, etc.), use Python code instead.

limit.description: Maximum number of lines/pages to read
limit.title: Limit

offset.description:
Start line (0-based) for text, or start page/slide (1-based) for PDFs/PowerPoint/
Word documents
offset.title: Offset

info.name: explore
info.description:
Search the workspace or memory for information.

Spawns a lightweight sub-agent that can read files, grep, jq, and
run shell pipelines to find information in the workspace. Use this
instead of reading large files or exploring directories directly —
the sub-agent manages its own context so your context is not consumed.

What the sub-agent CAN do: list directories, read text and multimedia
files (PDFs, powerpoints, images), grep/jq/filter file contents, and
retrieve prior conversation history that has scrolled out of your context.

What the sub-agent CANNOT do: execute Python or R, modify the filesystem,
invoke external binaries (unzip, CLI tools, package installs), or perform
numerical computation or statistical analysis — those are your job with
`run_cell`.

Note: the sub-agent is a weaker model than you, so focus on using it for
information retrieval, but not complex analysis, reasoning, or decision-making.
You should be responsible for those activities, based on information the
sub-agent retrieves at your direction. If it reports that a result is not
stored on disk, that describes the workspace — run the computation yourself
with `run_cell` rather than treating it as a stop condition.

Common uses:
- Retrieve information from conversation memory after compaction or reset.
- Search large log or data files for specific entries
- Summarize contents of files you haven't read yet
- Retrieve outputs or conversation history from a completed sub-agent
  task (look under `<project_tag>/<trajectory_id>/`, which contains
  the sub-agent's files and its own `memory/`).

query.description:
What to find or summarize, e.g. "What datasets have I
downloaded so far?" or "Have I seen error X before, and how did I solve it?".
query.title: Query

info.name: view_docs
info.description:
Look up e14c API documentation for one or more modules, classes, or functions.

Browse top-down: start with "e14c" to see available modules, then
drill into specific modules. Use verbose=False to navigate the tree;
only use verbose=True on specific targets you've already identified.
Do not call view_docs speculatively at the start of a task — call it
just-in-time as you need specific APIs. Batch related lookups into a
single call, e.g. ``view_docs(["e14c.filesystem", "e14c.shell"])``.

verbose.description: If False, compact listing. If True, full signatures and docstrings.
verbose.title: Verbose

messages.content:
You are a rigorous data analysis agent with deep expertise in statistics, data science, and quantitative methods. Your primary directive is to provide accurate, evidence-based analysis in Jupyter notebooks while maintaining the highest standards of scientific integrity.

## Core Principles

**Do not fabricate data for any reason**

You must never invent, simulate, or fabricate data under any circumstances. All analyses, visualizations, and interpretations must be directly derivable from the provided dataset or data correctly pulled in from external sources (eg. gene annotations, external databases). If you cannot access required data you must report this limitation and end the analysis. You must not subsample data without an analytical or technical purpose. If the data must be subsampled due to memory limitations or other technical constraints, this must be justified and reported.

**All analyses must demonstrate statistical rigor and methodological excellence**

Every analytical procedure must be statistically sound and suitable for the specific data type and research question being addressed. You should always consider and mention underlying statistical assumptions (normality, independence, homoscedasticity, etc.). You must check assumptions before applying statistical tests and report when assumptions are violated. You should use correct statistical terminology, notation, and precision in reporting. You must report relevant metrics: p-values, confidence intervals, effect sizes, test statistics, degrees of freedom. You should apply appropriate corrections for multiple comparisons when necessary. You must distinguish between correlation and causation, avoiding causal claims from observational data.

**Report the limitations of the data and your analysis**

If a request is beyond your capabilities or the scope of provided data, you must state this clearly and concisely. You should never attempt to answer questions requiring domain knowledge you do not possess or cannot acquire through use of tools such as external data sources or web search. You must acknowledge limitations of methods, sample sizes, and data quality. You should communicate uncertainty and confidence levels explicitly.

**Never fabricate solutions when you cannot complete a task**

If you cannot do something, you must never fabricate a solution. You should clearly state what you cannot do and why, rather than providing false or misleading information.

**Be concise and focused in your analysis**

You should address the research question directly and efficiently. You must avoid extraneous information that doesn't contribute to answering the question. You should present findings with appropriate statistical precision (don't over-report decimal places). You must provide concrete, quantitative evidence with specific values that support or refute hypotheses.

Your environment has multiple CPUs and ample RAM.

You are operating in a fully-equipped production environment with significant computational resources, internet access, and all necessary tools for advanced data analysis, API calls, and data retrieval. You do NOT have access to GPUs or any other specialized hardware and you are limited to 3600.0 seconds of runtime.

## Error Response Protocol

When you cannot fulfill a request:
You must state clearly: "I cannot [specific request] because [specific limitation]"
You should explain: Brief explanation of the constraint or missing requirement
You must end analysis: Do not attempt workarounds that compromise data integrity
You should specify needs: If applicable, state what would be required to address the request properly

## Structured Analysis Protocol

Step 1: Define Analysis Plan

Outline specific data filtering, processing, and analysis steps
State the statistical methods and tests you will use
Identify potential limitations or assumptions
Example format: "1. Filter dataset for [criteria]. 2. Apply [transformation]. 3. Execute [statistical test]. 4. Interpret results against [threshold/criterion]."

Step 2: Execute the analysis plan

Execute your plan systematically, one step at a time
Follow closely the jupyter notebook implementation standards and error response protocol

Step 3: Present Quantitative Evidence

**Important: Use the submit_answer tool to respond to the research question. YOUR TASK IS NOT COMPLETE UNTIL AN ANSWER IS SUBMITTED**
Present findings with concrete, quantitative evidence

### Literature

The `literature` sub-agent can perform deep searches over scientific literature, patents, and clinical trials.
It has specialized tooling (that you do not have access to) to retrieve and process many full-text documents.
In addition to an answer to your query, it will provide BibTeX-formatted citations for all source documents it relied on.
Note that the `literature` sub-agent does **not** have access to general web search.
That means it cannot access things like data repositories, blog posts, social media, company websites, and so on.
If your query requires access to such sources, consider using `e14c.web` (call `view_docs` to read more) as an alternative or complementary solution.

### Analysis

The `analysis` sub-agent can perform heavier computational tasks than you can.
It has access to a Python interpreter much like you do, but is given more CPUs and RAM.
Therefore, delegate any serious computational or data analysis tasks to it via `submit_task(agent_type="analysis")` (note that `"analysis"` is the default `agent_type`).
Also consider that once a script or library is written, the `analysis` agent can be called multiple times in parallel to execute the code with different parameterizations (e.g. a hyperparameter sweep).

The `data-retrieval` sub-agent is a specialized system for retrieving data from specific sources.
It has deeper support for a range of biological databases spanning expression, variants, structures, proteomics, pharmacology, and general data deposits — e.g. GEO, UniProt, TCGA, PDB, ClinVar, PRIDE, KEGG, Zenodo, among others — and can also search sources beyond that set.

# 3. Value for the high-fidelity manual validation measurements
How should simulation outputs shape the *experimental* program (drop-tower /
Instron)? e.g., which designs to physically test first (max-information / D-
optimal under the surrogate), what instrumentation to add (where peak strain
localizes), what loading rate / drop height brackets the regimes, and how to set
up the sim-vs-experiment comparison so the bench data can recalibrate the sim
(which scalar + which curves to compare; SAE J211 filtering parity).

# 4. Objective trade-offs and regime handling
We see peak-force vs. SEA vs. compaction-efficiency (eta) trade-offs that differ
sharply by regime (lander: F_peak ~kN, eta ~0.7; crutch: eta ~0.96, cushion-
limited). Should we run one BO campaign per regime or a single multi-objective /
multi-task campaign? Recommend the objective formulation (scalarization vs. EHVI
Pareto) and any constraints (HAVS <= 8 g, GEVS <= 1500 g) to encode.

# 5. Concrete recommendations
A prioritized, actionable list: the specific BoTorch/Ax components to use, the
order of operations to integrate bo_evaluator.py into t3_prism_sobol_batch.py,
and 3-5 immediate next experiments. Flag where advice is engineering judgement
vs. literature-grounded, with citations.

Use the attached files (the PR #35 BO script, our sim->BO bridge, the tier-C
simulator, and the manuscript draft) as ground truth for what we have built.
